idiom_name: parent class owns the state; children register through their constructor and read an interface
implementation_notes: The standard library has no component tree, so the pattern is the hand-written structure: the parent type owns the shared value and a container of child handles, children register at construction (taking the parent by reference), and the parent alone enforces the invariant and notifies the UI. What replaces the classic structure is ordinary composition plus a registration call and a small callback type (std::function or a template parameter); the classic form is justified when the group invariant must hold across objects whose lifetimes the parent manages, for example a form section that guarantees exactly one active option. Because there is no framework to re-render, the parent should also expose a change hook (a callback or a small signal) that the owning view subscribes to.
pitfalls: Raw child pointers assume the parent outlives the children; document the order or store std::reference_wrapper/std::weak_ptr and check on use.
std::function callbacks allocated per child add overhead and defeat inlining - template the parent on the child type, or keep a plain function pointer when the callback is stateless.
Header-only registration invites double registration (a child added twice); assert uniqueness or use a set keyed by identity.

variants.name: Qt group objects (QButtonGroup / QActionGroup) with QObject ownership
variants.implementation_notes: With Qt in the stack the pattern becomes a toolkit feature: QButtonGroup owns the exclusive selection, children declare membership with addButton and an id, and the group clears the previously selected button itself, so the parent only reacts once through idClicked/checkedButton instead of wiring every child. QActionGroup does the same for menu and toolbar actions, and QObject parent-child ownership gives the family the lifetime rule the hand-written form has to invent. The classic hand-written parent is still justified for invariants Qt does not model (cross-field validation, non-widget state), but exclusivity, enable/disable propagation and the re-render are all better left to the toolkit.
variants.idiom_name: QButtonGroup/QActionGroup own exclusivity; QObject parent-child ownership carries lifetime
pitfalls: QActionGroup serves menus/toolbars and QButtonGroup widgets - mixing both kinds of children in one family needs both groups and a shared mapping.
A button added to the group but not parented to a widget (or added to a layout twice) renders wrongly even though the exclusivity works.
Removing a button from a group does not clear its checked state; update the model explicitly when children are recycled.
